newsitem.title: CANADA: Interfor says new parks to reduce harvest.
newsitem.headline: Interfor says new parks to reduce harvest.

text.p: International Forest Products Ltd said Monday that the creation of 23 new parks in southwest British Columbia would reduce its harvest in the short term but it believes the amount will be "manageable."

Interfor chief executive Robert Sitter said the plan would reduce the company's long-term yield in the area by about two percent a year but hoped to offset that ultimately in other ways. The company is the biggest harvester in the three timber-supply areas affected, accounting for about one million cubic meters of the four million cubic meters of wood harvested yearly, he said.
"We expect (the harvest) to go down but by a manageable amount. We hope that decline is temporary and we have the opportunity to increase it," he said.

Sitter said his company strongly supported the plan announced Monday because it balanced competing interests and provided certainty on the land base avaiable. The plan allocates 18.4 percent of the land base or 770,000 hectares for harvesting. He said some other forest industry officials were opposed to Interfor's decision to give up its claim to part of the Stoltmann Wilderness old-growth forest. But most of that area will remain open to logging.
"The loss of timber and jobs is manageable. It could have been a lot worse," Sitter said. He did not anticipate any job losses at Interfor itself.
New forest regulations, land-use policies and harvest reductions are expected to reduce the amount of timber cut across British Columbia by about one quarter from 1992 to 1997 or 1998, Sitter said.
Over the past four years Interfor's operating costs have risen 30 to 40 percent but Sitter said he believes they have peaked.
